title: Yemen Edges Toward a New War, and This One Could Be Worse
excerpt: After four years of fragile calm, Houthi missile strikes, a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, and military buildups along front lines are pushing Yemen toward a renewed conflict that analysts say could be deadlier and more destabilizing than the last.
body:
• Houthi ballistic missiles and drones struck displacement camps and military positions in Marib and Hadramawt provinces, killing at least 32 people in the deadliest escalation since the 2022 truce.
  • The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, threatening the Bab al-Mandeb strait — now critical for Saudi oil exports since the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted by the Iran war.
  • Saudi Arabia has carried out retaliatory airstrikes on Houthi-controlled Hodeidah port and, alongside U.S. forces, struck Iranian-backed militias in eastern Iraq.
  • The U.N. Special Envoy warned Yemen faces its greatest risk of large-scale conflict since the 2022 truce, with both sides building up forces along front lines.

The Truce Is Over in Everything but Name

Yemen's four years of relative calm are unraveling. The Iran-aligned Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones at displacement camps and residential neighborhoods in the city of Marib on August 8, killing two people and wounding 14, according to Reuters. A day earlier, at least 30 Yemeni government troops were killed in strikes on military camps in Marib and Hadramawt provinces — one of the deadliest escalations in months.

The Yemeni army responded on multiple fronts along the lines of contact. Both sides have been building up forces along a front line spanning from the Red Sea coast to the Saudi border, according to military officials and analysts.

"Since 2022, these are the most serious preparations for a conflict I've seen," said Baraa Shiban, a Yemeni analyst and associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute.

Why This War Would Be Different

The previous Yemen war, which began in 2015 when a Saudi-led coalition intervened against the Houthis, killed hundreds of thousands and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. A new conflict would unfold in a fundamentally altered landscape.

The Iran war has closed the Strait of Hormuz to much of Gulf oil traffic, forcing Saudi Arabia to reroute exports through Red Sea ports like Yanbu. The kingdom is planning to push Red Sea exports to about 9 million barrels a day over the next three years. But tankers leaving Yanbu for Asian markets must transit the Bab al-Mandeb strait — precisely where the Houthis have declared their blockade.

"The Houthis appear to be following a North Korean playbook, using recurring cycles of provocation to extract political and economic concessions," analyst Mohammed al Basha told CNN.

"All the red lines have been crossed, all the buttons have been pushed."

— Mohammed al Basha, Yemen analyst

Saudi Arabia Hemmed In

Saudi Arabia now faces threats from three directions: Houthi missiles from Yemen, drone attacks from pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, and renewed threats from Tehran. Over the past week, the Houthis struck two Saudi oil complexes on the Red Sea coast, with satellite imagery showing extensive damage to a facility in Jazan near the Yemeni border.

Riyadh had spent five months trying to avoid being drawn into the broader regional conflict, maintaining communication channels with Tehran even as Iranian drones targeted Saudi oil infrastructure. That restraint ended when Saudi and U.S. fighter jets carried out joint strikes against Iranian-backed militias in eastern Iraq.

The Saudi air force also targeted the port at Hodeidah, the largest under Houthi control, in retaliation for tanker attacks. According to Nawaf Obeid of King's College London, the Saudi military is far more capable than a decade ago, with integrated detection and engagement systems that "dramatically shorten the time between detection and engagement."

A Domestic Calculus Driving the Houthis

The Atlantic Council's Allison Minor, a former U.S. deputy special envoy for Yemen, argues that the Houthis' decision to escalate may be driven more by conditions inside Yemen than by the Iran war. Despite controlling territory where 75% of Yemen's 35 million people live, the Houthis control none of the country's oil and gas resources. Their economy depends on illicit oil sales, aggressive taxation, and a stranglehold on commercial activity.

The World Food Programme stopped food distributions in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen in January after the group detained aid workers. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has shifted from viewing Yemen's internationally recognized government as a negotiating body to bolstering it as an effective governing entity — a move the Houthis may interpret as the end of any negotiated path to controlling Yemen's resources.

What Comes Next

U.N. Special Envoy Hans Grundberg warned that Yemen faces its greatest risk of large-scale conflict since the 2022 truce. The U.N. Security Council urged restraint, warning that the violence risked drawing Yemen deeper into a wider regional confrontation.

For now, analysts expect the Saudi response to remain limited to airstrikes. But a large force of Yemeni fighters hostile to the Houthis is assembling in eastern Yemen's deserts, a regional source told CNN. If it advances, it would be backed by Saudi Apache attack helicopters.

Whether the Houthis can be bought off, as they have been before, remains unclear. What is clear is that the conditions that kept Yemen's war frozen are melting away.
nri_angle: A renewed Yemen war and Red Sea disruption would further destabilize global shipping routes and energy markets, compounding the economic impact of the Iran war on trade-dependent economies across Asia.
